rationale: A wins because it does the adult PR work: it finds three real lanes and then names the kill questions before a reporter does. A's line, "whether the 10% sits on top of, or absorbs, the Apple/Google in-app-purchase cut," is the sharpest proof test in either set. B has good bones, but "Discord's move signals monetization is coming for the whole server, not just the streamer" is a TED-talk thesis wearing a news angle costume.
gaps_in_A: "the long fight over platform take rates (the Apple/Google 30% standard, Epic v. Apple, Substack's 10%, Patreon's tiers)" imports outside context not supplied in the update; useful context, but it needs verification before it becomes pitch copy.
"Discord opens a paid tier inside community servers built on free membership" rests on "servers have historically been free communities," which is plausible but not in the facts provided.

"Discord turns 200M users into a payments business" overuses the platform-wide MAU number; A correctly questions this later, but the headline still implies more addressable payment volume than the update proves.
gaps_in_B: "it won't say how much they'll make" turns "no creator-earnings data is available yet" into a refusal narrative. That is a factual overreach, and journalists notice that kind of makeup.
"how this revenue stream fits alongside existing lines (ads, Nitro)" invents business-line context not supplied in the update. Nitro may be real-world knowledge, but it was not in the assignment.
"monetization is coming for the whole server, not just the streamer" is broad category fog and partly duplicates the server-owner monetization angle.
The fee angle does not ask the best kill question: whether Discord's 10% stacks on top of app-store fees in mobile transactions. Without that, the 10%-versus-30% contrast may collapse.
